Where it began

Courtney Walsh was born in Kingston, Jamaica, on 30 October 1962. He learned his cricket at the Melbourne club in Kingston, the same club as Michael Holding, and first made people sit up in 1979, when he took all ten wickets in an innings in a school match. Three years later he was playing first-class cricket for Jamaica.

In all he took 1,807 first-class wickets at 21.71 in 427 matches, and he gave Gloucestershire well over a decade of loyal service.

The player

His Test debut came against Australia at Perth in 1984. Over seventeen years he played 132 Tests and took 519 wickets at 24.44, with 22 five-wicket innings, three ten-wicket matches and a best of 7 for 37. He captained West Indies in 22 Tests, winning six, losing seven and drawing nine.

For years he was the dependable stock bowler in an attack that included Malcolm Marshall and Joel Garner, before taking the new ball himself. With Curtly Ambrose he formed one of the most feared opening pairs in the game; between them they took 421 wickets in 49 Tests together. In 2000 he went past Kapil Dev's 434 to become Test cricket's leading wicket-taker. The next year, at Port-of-Spain, he had Jacques Kallis leg before to become the first bowler to reach 500.

What made him special

Walsh stood about six foot six and used every inch of it to make the ball climb. His action was no thing of beauty, but it was economical, and with his natural athleticism it let him bowl long, accurate spells year after year. Wisden admired the way he could change his pace three ways without any change in his action. Even as he slowed down in later years, the wickets kept coming.

He was also a famously fair opponent. In a 1987 World Cup match against Pakistan he declined to run out the last batsman, Saleem Jaffar, who had wandered from his crease before the final ball. West Indies lost and went out of the tournament, but Walsh was widely praised, and a local fan gave him a hand-woven carpet.

Away from the middle

Wisden named him one of its Cricketers of the Year in 1987, and in 2010 he joined the ICC Cricket Hall of Fame alongside Joel Garner. He was awarded the Order of Jamaica, was named in 2004 among Jamaica's greatest cricketers, and called his autobiography Heart of the Lion. After playing he served as a West Indies selector, became Bangladesh's bowling coach in 2016 and later their interim head coach, and in 2020 took charge of the West Indies women's team.

And finally

Walsh made 936 Test runs at 7.55, and by the end crowds cheered every ball he faced, along with his grand, windmilling leave. Yet one of his most useful innings contained no runs at all: in 1999 he stayed with Brian Lara through a last-wicket stand that beat Australia. Not every hero needs to trouble the scorers.
